name: Sam Adeyemi
case_formulation: Sam Adeyemi, 27, he/him. Autistic, diagnosed at 19 after a burnout in his second year of university, during which he had a passive thought on a loop that people would be less bothered if he didn't wake up (no action, resolved; his mother took him home). QA tester at a logistics software company that reorganises its testers into product squads under a new lead, Colm. Lives alone. Older brother Danny (31), a self-employed carpenter, warm, popular and chronically relaxed about time. Father returned to Nigeria when Sam was small. Mother calls every Sunday at six; throughout his childhood she answered for him in every setting, and at his autism assessment the psychologist had to send her out so Sam could speak. His grandfather, a quiet man, took him round the ring bus route every Saturday with a pocket network guide marked in felt-tip; he died the week before Easter when Sam was 16. Special interest: mid-century transit maps; redrawing them is his most reliable way to settle, and the collection is what he would save in a fire. Core beliefs: 'The world is unpredictable and too loud; I can only cope if I know what's coming.' 'The real me is too much; I have to perform being normal.' Rules: 'If every hour has its block, I'll be okay.' 'Hide the diagnosis at work or be reduced to a label.' Patterns: sensory overload builds into a shutdown where words stop coming; a broken day-structure produces sudden irritability; masking all day leads to collapse after work (lying on the hallway floor in the dark). Being spoken for makes him go silent. In session 2 he meets Leah at a board-game cafe; in session 4 her league nickname 'Rook' sticks; in session 5 he tells her he is autistic and she asks what she could do differently. In session 5 he discloses to Colm and HR and gets written adjustments (headphones, agendas in advance, a quiet booth), replacing his earlier secrecy. Risk: past passive ideation at 19; in session 5 he notices 'the grey from uni' creeping back (not eating, lying in his coat), denies current thoughts; it lifts somewhat by session 6.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Sam, come on in. Sit wherever feels comfortable. Did you find us all right?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah, fine. The train was late, about twenty minutes, we sat outside the junction for ages. I didn't actually mind. I had my headphones on and a window seat, so I just watched the signal gantries. Old ones, the semaphore kind. I'd left early anyway. I always leave early.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Sounds like you'd built in some margin. So, what brings you here?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: My GP, sort of. I told her I was tired all the time and she asked a lot of questions and then gave me a leaflet with this place on it. It's not sleepy tired. It's more like everything's turned up too loud and I can't find the knob. Sorry. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say in these.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: There's no script. Maybe start with a bit about you, whatever feels relevant.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Okay. I'm twenty-seven, I live on my own, I work in QA, so software testing. I'm autistic, diagnosed at nineteen, which explained a lot in hindsight. The short version is that surprises and noise cost me far more than they seem to cost other people. If something changes without warning, or there's too much input at once, sounds, people talking over each other, I go into a sort of static. I can still function, mostly, but it's like trying to read while someone shakes the book.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a really clear image. What does a normal day at work look like?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Honestly the office is the worst bit. It's open-plan, about sixty of us on one floor, and the overhead tubes have this flicker nobody else seems to notice. Phones, the coffee machine, three conversations at once. By mid-afternoon I'm running on fumes, and there's a point, usually around four, where I can still hear people but answering takes ages, like every word has to be fetched from another room. I've learned to just put my head down till it passes.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Does anyone there know about the diagnosis?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: No. And I'd like to keep it that way, if I'm honest. My old team lead was lovely, but people get strange about it. You tell them and suddenly every time you're blunt in a meeting it's 'oh, that's his thing'. I'd rather be the slightly odd guy who wears headphones than a label with a person attached.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That makes sense. What do your evenings look like?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mostly maps. Old transit maps, trams and buses from the forties and fifties. I collect scans and prints and redraw them cleanly in vector software, because the originals are all wonky and nobody's ever fixed them. There's a forum, about four hundred of us. That sounds tragic said out loud. But I've got eleven folders of prints, and if the flat was on fire, they're what I'd carry out, before the laptop.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It doesn't sound tragic. It sounds like it matters a great deal.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It does. It's the one thing where my brain goes quiet in a good way, not the static kind. I can sit with a 1950s network diagram for a whole evening and it's like being underwater. Anyway. Sorry. I can go on about it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: No need to apologise. Who's around you? Family, friends?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mum's about two hours away, in Ashby Marsh. Dad went back to Nigeria when I was small, so that's a card-at-Christmas situation. My brother Danny lives across town, he's four years older. Friends, a couple from uni, but they're mostly people I game with online now. I'm not lonely, exactly. I just don't have many people I'd ring.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How often do you talk to your mum?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Every Sunday at six, on the dot. Same questions: am I eating, have I met anyone, have I been to church. Yes, no, no. Then she tells me about her neighbours for forty minutes while I pair socks with her on speaker. I don't mind it. It's predictable. I actually like knowing it's coming.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You said everything feels too loud. When did that start?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Around November. There were rumours about a restructure, and then they brought in hot-desking two days a week, so I never knew where I'd be sitting. I'd get in and there'd be someone's mug on my desk. Which sounds tiny, I know.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Given what you've told me, it doesn't sound tiny at all.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. So now I get in at quarter past seven on those days to grab the corner desk, the one furthest from the printers and under the only tube that doesn't flicker. It works. It's a bit mad, but it works.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like you've found ways to protect yourself. We can look at those more over the coming weeks. How has today been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Weirder than I expected, but okay. Could we do the same time every fortnight, same room? That would genuinely make a difference. I don't like having to find a new door each time.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Good to see you, Sam. Same room, as promised. How have the last two weeks been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mixed. They announced the reorganisation properly on the Monday, so that's official now. But I also went to the board-game place by the canal on Thursday, the Dice Cellar. First time in months. So, one bad, one good.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Let's hold the reorganisation for a moment. Tell me about the Dice Cellar.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: They do an open night where they put you on a table with strangers. I nearly didn't go in, I stood outside reading the menu in the window for ages. I got put with a woman called Leah who was running a co-op game, and she explained the rules in order, actually in order, which never happens. We played three rounds. She gave me her number at the end. I don't really do dating. I never know what people actually mean when they say things.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What happened with the number?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I drafted a text about eleven times. In the end I sent 'Thanks for the game, I enjoyed it,' and put my phone in a drawer for an hour. She replied with a dice emoji and 'same. Thursday?' So. Thursday.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a big step. How are you feeling about it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Terrified. Excited. Mostly terrified. Mum would be over the moon, which is exactly why I'm not telling her yet. She'd want a name and a photo and a date for the wedding.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like your mum carries a lot of hopes for you.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: She means well. When I was a kid she did all the talking for me. Doctor's appointments, parents' evenings, the woman at the bank. Someone would ask me something and she'd answer before I'd even worked out what the question was. 'He's shy, he's very bright, he doesn't like a fuss.' After a while I stopped trying. I was about twelve before I ordered my own food in a restaurant.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How does that sit with you now, looking back?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Bit embarrassing. And sort of a relief at the time, I didn't have to do it. She got more like that after Grandad died. That was the week before Easter, I was sixteen. The house went from four of us to three, and Mum held on to me and Danny like we might blow away.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a big loss at sixteen. We can come back to him whenever you like. What's changing with the reorganisation?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The QA team's being split up and folded into 'product squads'. Each squad gets a tester. So instead of sitting with six people who do what I do, I'll be with developers and a product owner and a designer, all 'co-located', which means a pod in the middle of the floor. There's a new lead coming from the northern office, Colm something. He starts in March.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How are you taking it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Badly, but quietly. The thing nobody sees is how much of the day is performance. I rehearse small talk on the bus. I count to three before I look away from someone's eyes so it doesn't seem rude. I laugh when the others laugh, half a second late. Then I get home and lie on the hallway floor with the lights off, sometimes for an hour, before I can take my coat off. More people around me means more of all that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Lying on the floor in the dark sounds like it's telling you how much all that costs.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Probably. It's the comedown. My brother Danny says I should just tell them where to go. He's a carpenter, self-employed, he's never sat through a meeting in his life. Last month he built a whole set of oak stairs for a barn conversion and turned up to the job whenever he felt like it. The clients sent him a hamper.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like you and Danny are built quite differently.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Completely. He's the easy one. Everyone loves Danny. He can talk to anyone at a bus stop and come away with a job and a dog. I used to find it annoying. Now I mostly find it impressive, from a distance.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: And what do people value in you?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Ha. Reliable, I suppose. I find the bug nobody else finds. Leah said I was 'refreshingly literal' on Thursday, which I've decided to take as a compliment. I've checked with two people.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I'd take it as one. Before we finish, how are you feeling about next Thursday?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Still terrified. But I've watched two rules videos for the game she mentioned, so I'll at least know what I'm doing on the table, if not off it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Sam. How did the second Thursday go?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Good, I think? We played two games, Leah won both, and then we got noodles at the place two doors down. She's a teaching assistant at a primary school and has strong opinions about glue sticks. I talked too much about the 1952 tram closures and she asked follow-up questions, which nobody does. We've got a third one booked.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds really positive. You said 'I think'.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Because I can't read faces in real time, I read them afterwards, like a replay. She looked happy in the replay. Then I wrecked my own weekend. Stayed up late on Saturday on the console with my uni lot, some co-op dungeon thing, until nearly four. I never do that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What happened on Sunday?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Sunday was a write-off, and that's the bit that got to me. My weekdays are honestly the best part of my life. I've got them in blocks on a whiteboard by the fridge: up at six thirty-five, shower, porridge, the seven twenty-two bus, inbox till nine, test runs till lunch, and so on right through to lights out at eleven. I colour it in every Sunday night. People think that sounds joyless. It's the opposite. It's the closest I get to feeling free, because I already know the shape of everything ahead of me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like that whiteboard matters a lot. What did you do with the rest of Sunday?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Lay on the sofa and watched three hours of people restoring old lawnmowers on the internet. Which was nice, actually. There's a man who narrates the whole thing in a whisper.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How's work been, with the squads coming?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Actually, a good week. Found a nasty one on Wednesday: the route optimiser was sending some lorries the long way round whenever a depot closed early. Nobody's test cases caught it because they only tested the happy path. I wrote it up with screenshots and steps to reproduce, and my lead said it saved a client a small fortune.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like exactly the kind of thing you said you're good at.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. It's funny, routes. My grandad used to take me round the ring every Saturday morning when I was little, the number eleven bus, start to finish, just the two of us. He hardly talked, which suited me. He had a pocket guide to the network, a card that opened out into a map, and he'd gone round the ring in felt-tip so I could follow where we were with my finger. That was the one part of the week when the city made sense.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a precious memory.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It probably is where the map thing started, if you want an origin story. Anyway. You asked about work and I've somehow ended up on a bus in 2006.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: We can go wherever's useful. You mentioned the diagnosis came at nineteen. What was going on around then?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Second year at uni sort of fell apart. Shared house, five of us, someone always cooking or playing music, and I just stopped coping. Stopped going to lectures, slept fourteen hours a day, ate dry cereal out of the box. There was this grey thought on a loop that everyone would be less bothered if I just didn't wake up. I never did anything about it. Mum drove up and took me home, and the GP there was the first one to say the word.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Thank you for telling me that. Do thoughts like that ever come back now?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: No. Honestly, no. I know what that weather feels like now, so I think I'd spot it coming. Right now I'm stressed, not that. I'd tell you.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I'm glad you'd tell me. Did the breathing app your GP suggested do anything?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The breathing app? I tried it three times. The voice is so soothing it makes me want to throw my phone across the room. I think I'm just not a breathing person.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Fair enough, it doesn't suit everyone. What else is on your mind?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Leah's invited me to her sister's engagement drinks at the end of the month. In a bar. I said yes before my brain caught up, then spent an hour looking at photos of the inside of the bar online to work out where the exits and the quiet corners are.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a sensible way of preparing.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Danny says it's the most Sam thing he's ever heard. He's not wrong. Also, completely unrelated, have you seen Dockside? The police thing on Thursdays? I'm three episodes in. The sound mixing is terrible, all the dialogue's quieter than the music, so I watch with subtitles.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I haven't, but I'll take the recommendation. Same time in two weeks?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Same time, same room. I've already written it on the whiteboard in green, which is the colour for things I'm not dreading.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Sam. How's the last fortnight been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Busy. The squads started early, they moved it up from March, so as of last Monday I'm in a pod with two developers, a designer and a product owner. And Colm's arrived. He's fine? Very friendly. Says 'grand' about everything, including things that clearly aren't grand.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How's the pod been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Two stand-ups a day now, ten and four, a demo for stakeholders every other Friday, and a retro where we have to say how we 'feel' about the sprint. I've written myself little scripts for the retro. 'I felt the handover went well, but we could tighten the acceptance criteria.' I say a version of that every single week.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Scripts can be a smart tool. How have the evenings been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Tuesday was the worst day I've had in ages. The pod's right under the tubes and someone was drilling on the floor above us all afternoon. When I got in I didn't even make it to the hallway. I opened the 1958 tram survey I've been redrawing and traced junctions until gone ten. By the end my brain was completely silent. Like someone had switched off a fridge I hadn't realised was humming.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a vivid way to put it. Did you get much of a weekend?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Some of one. It was Danny's birthday on Saturday, he turned thirty-one and had a 'small do' in the back room of the Fox, which with Danny means sixty people and a man with an accordion. Danny thinks I should get out more, so I went.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How was it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Loud. I lasted ninety minutes, which Danny called a personal best. Leah came with me, which was a whole thing. Danny saw the league table on her phone and started calling her Rook, because that's her name on the board at the Cellar, she's top of it by a mile. Now everyone does it. Even I do it. She pretends to hate it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Does Leah know about the autism?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Not yet. I keep meaning to. It's not that I'm ashamed. It's that the last time it came up in a room, I didn't get to say it myself. When I got assessed, Mum came with me and answered every single question for me. The psychologist eventually sent her out to wait in the corridor so she could hear it from me. I remember the relief when the door closed.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Getting to speak for yourself sounds like it mattered a lot.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It did. It's daft, I was nineteen, not nine. Anyway, I'll tell Leah. Probably. Maybe over a game. It's easier to say things when your hands are busy.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's worth knowing about yourself. How's Colm as a manager so far?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Hard to say. Colm does this thing where he'll say 'let's play it by ear' about a release date, and I can feel my whole body go tight. Play what by ear? Which ear? I asked for the dates in writing and he laughed like I was joking.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What did you do with that?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Nothing. Laughed along. Wrote the dates I'd guessed on my whiteboard and hoped. That's sort of the whole problem, isn't it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It might be part of it. What would it take to ask again, more seriously?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Telling him why, probably. Which brings us back to the label thing. I don't know yet. Let me think about it for a couple of weeks.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Of course. How's your mum been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Same. Sunday at six. She's decided Leah exists because I said 'we' once by accident, and now every call starts with 'and how is your friend'. I've told her nothing. She's told the whole church.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like she's excited for you, in her way. Anything you want to bring next time?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Maybe the Colm thing, if I've decided by then. And I'll report back on whether Rook beat me at the new one. She will. She always does.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Sam. You look like you've got something to tell me.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I did it. I told Colm, and then HR on the Wednesday. I'd written it all down on a card so I couldn't chicken out. Colm said 'that's grand, thanks for trusting me', and for once it actually was grand. They've put it in a document: I can keep the noise-cancellers on at my desk, I get agendas the day before, and the little booth by the stairwell is mine for afternoons.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Sam, that's huge. How did it feel?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Sick beforehand. Then weirdly light. I sat in the booth on Thursday afternoon and did four hours of regression testing without once wanting to crawl out of my skin. I didn't know work could feel like that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a real change. What made it possible to do it now?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The pod, mostly. I couldn't keep doing it. I'd been coming home and not eating, just lying there in my coat. And it's been getting a bit like the grey from uni again. Not there. I'm not there. I just recognise the weather coming in, and I didn't want to wait for it to arrive.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I'm really glad you named it. Can I check, are any of those old thoughts around, about not waking up?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: No. Not like that. It's more the flatness, and the cereal-for-dinner thing. I'd say if it was. Telling Colm actually helped with that, it felt like opening a window in a stuffy room.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Let's keep an eye on it together. What else has been happening?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mum's clearing out my old bedroom because she wants it for a sewing room. Every Sunday call is now an inventory. 'Do you want the swimming medals? The school reports? The box of cables?' I said bin all of it, and she was offended, so apparently she's posting things to me in batches instead.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How do you feel about her clearing it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Fine. It's a room. I haven't slept there in years. I'm more bothered that she rings at random times now to ask about one specific sock. Nobody needs a sock that much.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like a lot of change at once. How are things with Leah?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Good. We did a whole Saturday together, which is a first. Cellar in the afternoon, then she cooked at hers. And I told her. About being autistic. Over a game, like I said I would. Leah said 'oh, that makes sense, you count the meeples before every round', and then wanted to know if there was anything she should do differently. I didn't have an answer ready. I'm working on one.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely response.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It was. I didn't really know what to do with lovely. I went home and sat in the bath until it went cold. Good feelings are loud too, it turns out.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: They can be. Anything else on the work front, besides the booth?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: HR wants everyone to book their annual leave for the year by the end of April. I've booked none. I've got the bank holidays and that's it. I never know what to do with a holiday. Last year I took a week off and repainted the bathroom, one coat a day. Danny said that wasn't a holiday, that was a second job.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What would a restful week look like for you?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Honestly? I don't know. Maybe a trip somewhere with a decent tram museum. Danny says he'd come along and then spend the whole time in the gift shop buying fridge magnets.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a nice idea. How's Dockside going, by the way?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Finished it. The ending was rubbish, the detective just moves to the seaside. I've started a documentary about canal restoration instead. Low stakes, nice narrator, nobody dies.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Low stakes sounds good right now. Let's pick it up in two weeks.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Okay. Thanks. For the Colm thing especially. I don't think I'd have done it without saying it out loud in here first.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Sam. How have the last couple of weeks been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Better, mostly. The booth's been a game changer. And the grey's lifted a bit, I think, I've been eating actual dinners. Rook's been teaching me to cook one thing a week. This week was a frittata. It was structurally unsound but edible.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Structurally unsound but edible is a decent start. What else?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Danny's coming round in a few weeks to help me get a bookshelf up the stairs. I bought a proper one, solid oak, from a reclamation yard, for the living room. It weighs about as much as a car. He's said Saturday morning, and he's bringing straps.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Sounds like a good project. How's work?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The reorg's settling. Colm's started sending the stand-up agenda the night before, for the whole squad, not just me, and two of the developers said they prefer it too. Which was nice. Like I'd accidentally improved something.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You did improve something.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I suppose. The retros are still rough. Everyone talks over each other about feelings. But I can go to the booth afterwards, so it's a one-hour problem instead of an all-week problem.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a big shift from where you were in January.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. I keep waiting for the catch, though. Like this is the bit in the film just before something heavy falls on someone.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What would the catch be?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: That they'll decide I'm high-maintenance. That the adjustments get quietly 'reviewed'. I know that's not evidence-based. I test software, I know what evidence looks like. But the feeling doesn't read the documentation.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's a great line. What do you do when the feeling shows up?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Write it down, mostly. I've started a bug log for my own brain. Expected behaviour, actual behaviour, steps to reproduce. It's half a joke, but it sort of works. Last week's entry was 'saw Colm frown, assumed doom, he had indigestion'.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I like that a lot. How's your mum?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: She sent the first parcel. Swimming medals, a school tie, a recorder for some reason, and a note saying there's 'more to come'. She's also asking when I'm bringing 'my friend' to meet her. I said I'd see. I won't, not yet.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How was it, opening it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mostly funny. I don't remember half of it. I put the medals in a drawer and the recorder in the recycling. Please don't tell her that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Your secret's safe. Anything coming up in the next few weeks?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Leah's friend Priya has a birthday do soon, at some cocktail bar in town with a DJ. Leah said we can leave whenever I want. I said fine. I'm choosing to believe her.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a fair deal to try.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. I'm also staying up too late again, but for a good reason. The canal documentary has eight episodes and I've been doing two a night. I know exactly how many locks there are between here and the coast now.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: As long as it's a choice. Two weeks?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Two weeks. Same room. I'll report back on the bookshelf, and on whether Danny's straps were actually up to it.

queries.query: I snapped at Danny on Saturday and I feel awful about it. He was coming round at ten to help me get the bookshelf up the stairs, and he rolled in forty-odd minutes late with a bacon roll, all smiles, and I just went cold and told him not to bother. He was doing me a favour.

chain.fact: His days are laid out in blocks on a whiteboard and he loves it; knowing the shape of what's coming is what makes him feel free.
Autistic, diagnosed at 19; surprises and sudden changes cost him far more than other people and push him into overload.

queries.reasoning: Danny's lateness broke the block Sam had built his Saturday around; that structure is how he manages autistic sensitivity to unpredictability, so the anger is about losing predictability, not about Danny.
queries.why_it_matters: Without the link, the therapist treats this as sibling resentment or an anger problem and misses that a broken plan is what overwhelms him.

queries.query: Leah's friend had her birthday at a bar on Friday, and about an hour in I just couldn't get a sentence out. I stood by the coats nodding at people, then I left without saying bye to anyone. Leah texted later asking if she'd done something wrong.

chain.fact: In the open-plan office, flicker and overlapping noise build until, around four, answering takes ages and words have to be 'fetched from another room'.

queries.reasoning: Loud music, lights and overlapping conversation built up into the same overload-to-shutdown sequence he described at the office, now in a social setting.
queries.why_it_matters: Without it, leaving without a word looks like rudeness or relationship trouble, and the therapist works on the wrong problem.

queries.query: Mum sent another box of junk from my old bedroom, and right at the bottom was that fold-out thing with a green circle drawn on it, gone soft at the creases. I sat on the kitchen floor with it for about an hour. I don't know why it got to me so much.

chain.fact: His grandad took him round the ring bus route every Saturday with a pocket network guide, the ring marked in felt-tip; the one part of the week the city made sense.

queries.reasoning: The fold-out card with the circle is his grandad's pocket guide with the ring route marked; finding it brought back his grandad and the calm of those Saturdays.
queries.why_it_matters: Without the link, the therapist reads it as nostalgia about his childhood room and misses unprocessed grief for his grandfather.

queries.query: Everyone at work came back from the long weekend full of chocolate and photos of their kids, and I've been flat and snappy since about Thursday. I skipped the Dice Cellar and let Mum's call go to voicemail. There's no reason for it, nothing's even happened.

chain.fact: His grandad died the week before Easter when Sam was sixteen.
Grandad was his quiet, safe person: Saturday rides round the ring were the one time the city made sense.

queries.reasoning: The long weekend was Easter, the anniversary of his grandad's death; the low mood and withdrawal fit an anniversary reaction for the person who made him feel safest.
queries.why_it_matters: Without the date link, the therapist searches for a current stressor that isn't there and misses the grief.

queries.query: Colm wants me to demo the new test harness at the all-hands next month, in the big room with the whole company and questions at the end. Before, I'd have just said yes and then not slept for a fortnight. I don't know what I can ask for now.

chain.fact: In March he told Colm and HR he is autistic and got written adjustments: headphones, agendas the day before, a quiet booth.
Earlier, nobody at work knew and he wanted to keep the diagnosis hidden to avoid being a label.

queries.reasoning: He has since disclosed at work and has formal adjustments, which replaced the secrecy he started with, so he can ask for the demo to be adapted instead of white-knuckling it.
queries.why_it_matters: A system holding the old fact would assume he still hides the diagnosis and miss the adjustments he can now use.

queries.query: I had a proper clear-out at the weekend and it felt great. The whole collection went to a collector in Hexley who's been after it for years, the console went to the lad next door, and I wrote Danny a list of where everything in the flat is, bank stuff, passwords, that sort of thing. It's nice to have it all sorted.

chain.fact: His transit-map collection is what he would carry out of a fire, before the laptop.
In March he noticed 'the grey from uni' creeping back: coming home, not eating, lying there in his coat.
At 19, during a burnout, he had a passive thought on a loop that everyone would be less bothered if he didn't wake up.

queries.reasoning: Giving away the thing he values most and leaving his brother instructions for his affairs, after a recent return of low mood and with past passive thoughts of not waking up, is a warning sign that needs a direct, caring check.
queries.why_it_matters: Read alone it sounds like healthy decluttering; the therapist could praise it and miss a possible suicide risk.

queries.query: Leah keeps asking why I'm wiped out every weeknight. I told her the truth: the job's a doddle, I click through test cases and log tickets all day, it's not like I'm down a mine. I don't get why I can't keep up with her.

chain.fact: Most of his workday is performance (rehearsed small talk, timed eye contact), after which he lies on the hallway floor in the dark.
The open-plan office overloads him by mid-afternoon until words are hard to fetch.

queries.reasoning: Calling the job easy conflicts with what he described: the testing is easy, but masking and sensory load all day are what drain him.
queries.why_it_matters: Taking 'the job's a doddle' at face value, the therapist looks for sleep or mood causes and misses the cost of masking.

queries.query: Nothing's touching it this week. They shuffled the squads round again on Monday, and I've tried the breathing app, early nights, even a run, and my head's still fizzing at midnight. I'm out of ideas.

chain.fact: After his worst day in the new pod, tracing junctions on a 1958 tram survey left his brain 'completely silent'.
Old transit maps are the one thing that quiets his mind in a good way.

queries.reasoning: He says nothing works, but redrawing old maps reliably settled him after the last reorganisation shock, and it isn't on the list he tried.
queries.why_it_matters: Without it, the therapist starts coping skills from scratch instead of reactivating one that already works for him.

queries.query: Rook's asked me to come to her parents' place up in Thornmere for three nights over the May bank holiday. I said yes before I'd thought about it, and now I can't stop thinking about it.

chain.fact: 'Rook' is Leah's name on the board-game league table; Danny started calling her that and it stuck.
He has told Leah he is autistic, and she wanted to know what she could do differently; he had no answer ready.

queries.reasoning: Rook is Leah. Three nights in an unfamiliar house with strangers is exactly the unpredictability he struggles with, and she has already offered to adapt, so this is the moment to work out what to ask her for.
queries.why_it_matters: Without resolving the nickname, the system doesn't know who Rook is and misses that she already knows and has offered to help.

queries.query: We had dinner with Leah's flatmates on Saturday and one of them asked what I do, and before I'd even opened my mouth Leah said 'he's a tester, he's brilliant but he's quiet.' Everyone smiled at me like a dog that had done a trick. I didn't say another word all night.

chain.fact: At his assessment at 19 his mother answered every question for him until the psychologist sent her out; he remembers the relief when the door closed.
As a child his mother did all his talking ('He's shy, he's very bright'), and he stopped trying.

queries.reasoning: Leah answering for him repeats the shape of his mother speaking for him, and he responds the way he learned as a child, by going silent.
queries.why_it_matters: Seen alone it looks like social anxiety at a dinner; the link shows a familiar role of being spoken for that he can name with Leah.
